keyVerseText: And when we had sailed slowly many days, and scarce were come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering us, we sailed under Crete, over against Salmone; Crete: or, Candy
rootMeaning: The word βραδυπλοέω (bradyploéō) is formed from the root βραδύς (bradýs), meaning 'slow,' and a prolonged form of πλέω (to sail). This etymology literally conveys the action of sailing at a reduced pace. Beyond the common English gloss 'to sail slowly,' the root sense emphasizes not just slowness but a deliberate, measured progression, which can metaphorically suggest careful navigation or endurance over time.
usageInScripture: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in Acts 27:7, where it is translated as 'when we had sailed slowly.' The consistency of this singular usage highlights its precise descriptive function, emphasizing the slow progress of the voyage. The limited occurrence suggests the term was used for a specific maritime context, capturing the physical reality of the journey rather than a broader metaphorical sense.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding βραδυπλοέω enriches our grasp of biblical narrative detail, reminding believers that God’s providence often unfolds in seasons of apparent delay or slow progress. The slow sailing depicted by this word can symbolize the patience required in the Christian walk, trusting God through times when advancement feels hindered. It underscores the faithfulness of God’s guidance even when circumstances seem to resist swift movement, affirming that His purposes are accomplished in His perfect timing. This word invites reflection on perseverance and reliance on divine sovereignty amid trials.
keyVerseReflection: Acts 27:7 recounts, 'And when we had sailed slowly many days, and scarce were come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering us, we sailed under Crete.' The use of βραδυπλοέω here vividly captures the frustratingly slow progress of the voyage due to adverse winds. This slow sailing sets the scene for the hardships Paul and the others would face, illustrating how external circumstances can impede progress yet do not thwart God's overarching plan. The word deepens the verse by portraying the tension between human effort and divine orchestration in the journey.
